transcript.text: Every so often when I use the hob the electrics in the house go off. Not every time, maybe once a week. It's an induction hob, Hisense I think.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. A hob that knocks the house electrics off is usually the safety protection reacting to current leaking to earth, even if it only happens once a week. Please don't use the hob again until a qualified engineer has checked it. Turn it off at its isolator switch, or at its breaker in the fuse box, and leave it off. Intermittent earth faults tend to get worse, not better. 1. An induction coil or the power module (the electronics that drive the coils) leaking to earth. 2. Moisture or a spill getting under the glass or into the electronics, for example after a boil-over or a heavy wipe-down. This also tends to be on-and-off.
3. A loose, scorched or damp connection at the hob's mains terminal block, or a fault in the power side of the control board. You can help the engineer pin it down without touching anything inside. The induction electronics can hold a dangerous charge even when switched off, so leave all covers alone.
1. Next time you're at the fuse box, note which switch had dropped. If it's the RCD (often marked with a 'T' test button), that points to earth leakage in the hob. If it's a single breaker, that can mean overload or a short on that circuit.
2. Did they happen on a particular zone, when using boost or high power, or after a spill or cleaning? One zone points to that coil or its part of the power module. After a spill points to moisture. Straight away at switch-on points more to the wiring or connection.
3. With the hob switched off at the isolator and cool, look at the glass and the visible edges for cracks, chips, or any brown or scorched marks, and notice any hot-plastic or burning smell. Mention anything you find to the engineer. Repairing coil, module and wiring faults is engineer work on any induction hob. If the hob is fairly new, check whether it's still under the Hisense warranty first, as that may cover it. Which switch dropped, and is there a pattern to when it happens?

Not sure which switch it is, but a big switch in the middle of the fuse box drops. It's usually when I've got two rings on high, and a couple of times it was during a boil-over. I did notice a faint electrical smell once after it tripped.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. That pattern is really useful, and the smell settles one thing: the hob mustn't be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it. Keep it off at its isolator or breaker. A big switch in the middle of the fuse box is very often an RCD, which trips when current leaks to earth rather than when a circuit is overloaded. Your two triggers fit two likely culprits: 1. A poor or overheating connection, either at the hob's mains terminal block, the supply cable or the power side of the hob's electronics. Running two rings on high pulls the most current, and the electrical smell after a trip suggests something got hot. This is my front runner.
2. Moisture from the boil-overs getting into the electronics under the glass. Water tracking to earth is a classic cause of on-off RCD trips, especially soon after a spill.
3. An induction coil or power module whose insulation is breaking down, so it leaks to earth only when it's working hard. The cause may also be more than one of these, because heat and moisture together make leakage worse. Telling them apart needs proper insulation testing with the covers off, which is engineer work. Induction electronics can hold a dangerous charge even when switched off. Things you can safely do to help:
1. Look at that big switch without touching anything inside the box. A 'T' or 'Test' button, or RCD/RCCB printed on it, suggests it's earth leakage. If it's at one end of the board and labelled 'Main switch', mention that, as it would be unusual and worth the electrician seeing.
2. With everything off, look at the hob's isolator switch and its wall plate for any browning, melting or scorch marks. Marks there point strongly to the connection, which is an electrician's job rather than a hob repair.
3. Write down the pattern for the engineer: two rings on high, the boil-overs, the smell and roughly once a week. It saves diagnosis time. Get an appliance engineer who works on induction hobs. If the isolator or supply looks scorched, get an electrician as well. If the hob is fairly new, check the Hisense warranty first. If it's older and the power module turns out to be the problem, ask for a quote before agreeing, as that repair can come close to the cost of a new hob. Does the big switch have a 'T' test button or say RCD on it?
I haven't looked at it closely, I don't know about a T button. Is that something I need to go and check? I'm not sure what RCD means.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
No, you don't need to check it. It would only confirm what the engineer will find out anyway, so don't worry about it. RCD stands for residual current device. It's a safety switch in your fuse box that constantly compares the electricity going out to a circuit with the electricity coming back. If some goes missing, usually because it's leaking to earth through water, damaged insulation or, at worst, a person, it cuts the power in a fraction of a second. It's there to stop shocks and fires. On many fuse boards it's a big switch in the middle, which is why I suspect that's what has been dropping. That would fit a hob leaking current to earth when it's working hard or wet, rather than simply overloading the circuit. If you're curious, reading the front of the switch is safe, as long as you don't open or touch anything inside the box. But it isn't needed. The hob must stay off until a qualified engineer has checked it. My order of suspicion hasn't changed: an overheating connection first (because of the smell and the two-rings-on-high pattern), then moisture from the boil-overs, then a coil or power module breaking down. 1. If the hob is fairly new, contact Hisense support first, as a warranty repair costs you nothing.
2. Otherwise, book an appliance engineer who works on induction hobs. 3. If there are any brown or melted marks on the hob's isolator switch or its wall plate, get an electrician too, as that would point to the supply wiring.
